content.title: About
content.content: The Barbecue Sandwich is a hot sandwich featuring a tender beef steak, smothered in a smoky barbecue sauce, melted cheese, crispy onions and pickles. It belongs to the NFS (New Food Series) line and is designed for quick service in cafés and food courts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sandwich was first launched in 2023 as part of the NFS range, aimed at modern taste preferences.
The barbecue sauce is made from a proprietary blend of smoked spices and a touch of honey.
Whole‑grain bread is used, retaining its crunch even after heating.
Each sandwich contains 150 g of beef steak, making it more protein‑rich than typical chicken variants.
It is commonly served with fries or a fresh side salad.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef steak provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat supplies easily absorbable iron, supporting hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc from the meat helps maintain a healthy immune system.

items.title: Includes vegetables
items.content: Pickles and onions add vitamin C and antioxidants.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of carbs and fats delivers quick energy.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The bread contains gluten, which may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Barbecue sauce and cheese can be salty; individuals with hypertension should limit portions.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Beef and cheese contain saturated fats that can affect cholesterol levels if consumed excessively.

items.title: Food safety risk
items.content: The sandwich should be served hot (at least 75 °C) to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich hot, straight from the grill. It can be cut in half for easier handling, and optionally topped with fresh lettuce or a drizzle of chili sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared sandwich refrigerated for no more than 2 hours at 4 °C. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for up to 1 month and reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned beans are cooked legumes sealed in an airtight jar with brine or tomato sauce. They retain most of their nutrients, are shelf‑stable, and cook quickly. Beans have a mild, slightly nutty flavor and a tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans belong to the legume family and include varieties such as kidney beans, chickpeas, lentils, and soybeans.
Canning of beans became widespread in the 19th century with the advent of metal cans.
When unopened, canned beans can be stored for several years at room temperature.
In many cultures canned beans are a staple side dish served with rice or added to soups.
Beans are a good source of plant protein and dietary fiber.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, making them an excellent protein source for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for hemoglobin formation and muscle‑nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned beans contain virtually no fat, fitting well into low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients in beans help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Many canned beans are packed with added salt, so people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Bacterial spoilage
items.content: Damaged or opened cans can harbor pathogenic bacteria if not handled properly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned beans can be tossed into salads, soups, stews, pasta dishes, or used as a filling for tacos and burritos. They heat quickly on the stovetop or in the microwave after draining the liquid.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, transfer beans to an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3–4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of lean beef, boiled rice, and vegetables (carrots, broccoli and/or dark‑green leafy greens). It is prepared without sauce, preserving the natural flavors of the ingredients and reducing added fats and sugars.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is an excellent source of complete protein containing all essential amino acids.
Rice is one of the world’s most consumed grains; it provides quick‑digesting carbohydrates that replenish energy rapidly.
Broccoli is rich in vitamin C and compounds that support the body’s detoxification processes.
Carrots are the primary source of beta‑carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A.
Dark‑green leafy greens (spinach, kale) contain iron, calcium, and folate, important for blood formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: Protein from beef aids muscle growth and repair, especially after physical activity.

items.title: Provides quick energy
items.content: Rice carbohydrates are rapidly absorbed, delivering fast energy to the brain and muscles.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Vitamin C in broccoli and beta‑carotene in carrots help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamins A and C, along with minerals from leafy greens, strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Calcium and vitamin K from leafy greens contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Excess red meat consumption
items.content: Eating large amounts of beef may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease if not balanced with plant foods.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the beef was pre‑marinated, sodium levels can be high; choose unseasoned meat or limit added salt.

items.title: Vegetable allergies
items.content: Rarely, individuals may be allergic to broccoli or carrots.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked beef can harbor pathogenic bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a complete meal. It can be portioned, garnished with a squeeze of lemon or fresh herbs, and paired with a light, unsauced salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags; reheat thoroughly before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Carrots are root vegetables belonging to the Apiaceae family. Raw carrots are commonly used in salads; they are crunchy, mildly sweet, and rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrots were domesticated in Central Asia over 5,000 years ago.
Originally carrots were purple; the orange variety was developed in the 17th century in the Netherlands.
Raw carrots are more than 90 % water and contain virtually no fat.
Beta‑carotene from carrots can improve night vision.
Carrots can be used as a natural food coloring.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in carrots is converted to vitamin A, supporting eye health and immune function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Carrots contain antioxidants (carotenoids, vitamin C) that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in raw carrots promotes regular bowel movements and overall digestive health.

items.title: May reduce cardiovascular risk
items.content: Potassium and antioxidants help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Skin health
items.content: Vitamin A and antioxidants contribute to healthy skin and its regeneration.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to carrots.

items.title: Digestive discomfort with excess intake
items.content: Large amounts of raw carrot can cause gas and bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic carrots, rinse them thoroughly to remove possible chemical residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw carrots can be cut into sticks, grated, or sliced into rounds for salads, snacks, and smoothies. They work well in vegetable mixes or as dippers for hummus and other spreads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store carrots in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, preferably in a perforated bag. When kept properly, they stay fresh for 2–3 weeks. Discard carrots that become soft, develop spots, or emit an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: A corn dog is a deep‑fried sausage on a stick coated with a cornmeal batter. The snack originated in the United States in the early 20th century and quickly became a favorite at fairs and carnivals. Its golden, crunchy crust pairs with a juicy meat interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial corn dog recipe appeared in the 1940s in Texas.
Traditional corn dogs use pork or beef sausages, but today chicken, turkey and vegetarian versions are common.
In the U.S. the Fourth of July often features corn‑dog eating contests.
The batter is usually made from cornmeal, wheat flour, sugar, salt and leavening agents.
Japan has its own twist on corn dogs, adding seafood and soy sauce.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The sausage provides animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The combination of batter and meat delivers fast‑acting calories for active lifestyles.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat supplies heme iron, supporting normal blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sausages contain vitamin B12 and niacin, which aid nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Cornmeal fiber
items.content: In modest amounts, cornmeal adds dietary fiber that benefits digestion.

items.title: High fat and sodium
items.content: Traditional corn dogs are deep‑fried and often contain a lot of saturated fat and salt, which can increase cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: One corn dog can contain 250–350 kcal, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The batter may contain gluten, and the sausage can include dairy or soy additives, important for people with allergies.

items.title: Trans fats from frying
items.content: Repeated use of frying oil can create trans fats, which are harmful to health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn dogs are usually served hot, straight from the fryer, with mustard, ketchup or a honey‑mustard sauce. The stick makes them easy to eat at picnics, fairs and sporting events.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked corn dogs in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days in an airtight container. For longer storage, freeze them in a sealed bag; reheat in an oven or fryer to restore a crisp crust before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Mixed nuts, honey roasted, is a blend of almonds, hazelnuts, cashews, walnuts and peanuts coated with a thin layer of honey glaze and lightly roasted to a golden hue. The nuts retain their characteristic flavors while the honey adds sweetness and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The honey glaze helps keep the nuts crunchy longer by slowing fat oxidation.
Mixed nut blends are popular in backpacking meals because of their high energy density.
Honey can be substituted with maple syrup for a vegan version.
Some mixes include dried fruit or spices, but this product uses only pure honey.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Nuts provide monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The nuts contain thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Honey and nuts are high in flavonoids and polyphenols that combat free radicals.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein, fiber and fat helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Nuts supply magnesium, phosphorus, zinc and iron, essential for many bodily functions.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: The product contains several types of nuts, which can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Honey‑roasted nut mixes are calorie‑dense, so moderation is recommended.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Honey adds natural sugars, which may be a concern for people with diabetes or low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Small nuts can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the honey‑roasted mixed nuts as a snack, stir them into granola, yogurt, baked goods, or sprinkle over salads for a crunchy boost.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For extended storage, refrigerate to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.

mozzarella-cheese-tomato-and-basil-with-.title: Mozzarella, Tomato and Basil with Oil and Vinegar Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: A fresh salad of mozzarella cheese, ripe tomatoes and fragrant basil, dressed with extra‑virgin olive oil and wine vinegar. The ingredients are simple, yet together they create a bright, summery flavor typical of Italian cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional mozzarella is made from water buffalo milk, but most commercial versions are cow‑milk based.
Basil is considered a symbol of love and happiness in Italy and is often used in wedding dishes.
Tomatoes, native to South America, only became a staple of Mediterranean cooking in the 16th century.
Cold‑pressed extra‑virgin olive oil retains most of the polyphenols that are beneficial for heart health.
Wine vinegar adds a gentle tang and helps improve iron absorption from tomatoes.

items.title: Rich source of calcium
items.content: Mozzarella provides a notable amount of calcium, which supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Antioxidants from tomatoes
items.content: Lycopene, abundant in tomatoes, has strong antioxidant properties and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil supplies monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Vitamins K and B group
items.content: Basil and tomatoes contribute vitamin K as well as B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Vinegar stimulates gastric juice production, aiding the digestion of the meal.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People sensitive to milk proteins or lactose may experience reactions.

items.title: Sodium content in ready‑made dressing
items.content: If using a pre‑made sauce, watch the salt level, especially for hypertension.

items.title: Acidity of vinegar
items.content: Excessive vinegar intake can irritate the stomach lining in individuals with gastritis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a standalone dish or as a side to pasta, fish or meat. Add arugula, toasted nuts or croutons for extra texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 2‑3 days. Store mozzarella in its brine and keep tomatoes separate to prevent excess moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: A muffin is a small, individual-sized quick bread, usually sweet, made from flour, eggs, sugar, butter or oil, and a leavening agent. It is a popular snack in cafés and for on‑the‑go consumption. Variations may include berries, nuts, chocolate, or spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Originally muffins were small bread‑like cakes baked in metal tins.
In the United States muffins are a common breakfast item, while in the United Kingdom the term “cup cake” is reserved for frosted versions.
There are more than 30 classic recipes, including banana, blueberry and chocolate varieties.
Muffins can be made gluten‑free or vegan by substituting wheat flour, eggs, or dairy.
Traditional English muffins are cooked on a griddle rather than baked.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates in muffins provide quick glucose for active lifestyles.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and eggs supply B1, B2 and niacin, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Rich in fiber (when whole‑grain ingredients are used)
items.content: Berries, nuts or whole‑grain flour increase dietary fiber, supporting digestion.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Blueberries, chocolate or spices such as cinnamon add antioxidant properties.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: Using plant oils or a modest amount of butter keeps fat levels within normal ranges.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet muffins can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Recipes often contain eggs, dairy, nuts and gluten, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of butter and sugar, muffins are calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Trans‑fat presence
items.content: Using margarine instead of natural fats can introduce small amounts of trans fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Muffins can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, sliced and topped with cottage cheese, yogurt or nut butter. They are convenient for travel and pair well with tea or coffee.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for 2‑3 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Warm before eating in a microwave or oven.

content.title: About
content.content: Tap water is drinking water supplied by municipal water systems. It undergoes treatment and disinfection to meet safety standards and be suitable for everyday consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In most countries tap water undergoes triple treatment: mechanical, chemical and biological.
Some regions add fluoride to tap water to help prevent cavities.
Mineral content (hardness) varies according to the geology of the area the water passes through.
Tap water is typically 30‑50 times cheaper than bottled water.
In many places tap water can be used for cooking without additional filtration.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Regular consumption of clean water maintains the body’s fluid balance, essential for all physiological processes.

items.title: Kidney function support
items.content: Adequate water intake helps flush metabolic waste and reduces the risk of kidney stone formation.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Water participates in breaking down food and facilitates nutrient absorption.

items.title: Skin health
items.content: Proper hydration contributes to skin elasticity and overall appearance.

items.title: Body temperature regulation
items.content: Sweating and evaporation of water help keep body temperature within a safe range.

items.title: Contamination
items.content: In some areas tap water may contain heavy metals, bacteria or chemical pollutants; it is advisable to check water quality.

items.title: Water hardness
items.content: High mineral levels can cause scale buildup on appliances and may lead to dry skin.

items.title: Chlorine and by‑products
items.content: Chlorine is commonly used for disinfection and can impart taste and cause irritation in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tap water can be consumed directly, after boiling, or filtered if quality is uncertain. It is also used for preparing beverages, meals, and household purposes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store water in a clean, sealed container, preferably glass or food‑grade plastic, in a cool place. For prolonged storage, replace the water every 2‑3 days.
